theme: Purity laws; the Nazirite vow; the Aaronic blessing
readingInstruction: Read Numbers 5:1-6:27. This reading includes some unusual laws about purity and suspicion, the Nazirite vow, and the best-known blessing in the Old Testament. Read the blessing at the end aloud.
settingTheScene: The camp is arranged, and now it has to be kept clean, because God lives in it. Chapter 5 deals with people who are unclean, with wrongs that need restitution, and with a ritual for a suspected case of unfaithfulness in marriage. Chapter 6 describes the Nazirite vow, a special period of consecration that anyone could take. The chapter ends with the words Aaron and his sons were to speak over Israel.
observation: People with skin diseases or discharges, or who have touched the dead, are sent out of the camp, “that they may not defile their camp, in the midst of which I dwell” (5:1-4).
A person who wrongs another must confess, make restitution, and add a fifth (5:5-10).
The ritual for a suspected wife is described in detail (5:11-31).
A Nazirite vows to abstain from wine and grape products, to let the hair grow, and to avoid contact with the dead (6:1-8).
If the vow is broken by accident, the Nazirite shaves and brings offerings (6:9-12).
At the end of the vow, offerings are made, and the hair is burned (6:13-21).
“The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace” (6:24-26).
“So shall they put my name upon the people of Israel, and I will bless them” (6:27).
interpretation:
The laws in chapter 5 continue the theme of God’s presence in the camp. Since the LORD dwells among them, anything that spoils the community’s purity is a serious matter. It is not just about private cleanliness. The people are one body, and the sin or uncleanness of one affects all.

The law about restitution is worth noting. Confession is not enough. A person who has wronged someone must pay back what was taken, plus a fifth, and the payment goes to the wronged person. True repentance has practical shape.

The suspected-adultery ritual is unusual and hard to understand today. It was designed to protect an accused woman from a husband’s jealousy by placing the matter in God’s hands. It was a way of keeping a suspicion from turning into violence, and it put the verdict in the hands of the God who sees all things.

The Nazirite vow is a different kind of consecration. Priests were born to their roles, but a Nazirite chose his. Any man or woman could set themselves apart for a time. The three signs of the vow, no grapes, uncut hair, and no contact with the dead, marked a life given wholly to God. It reminds us that holiness is available to everyone.

The blessing at the end is a gem. It has three lines, each longer than the one before, and each is a prayer for God’s favor: his protection, his face turned toward us, and his peace. The key phrase is “put my name upon the people.” The blessing is not Aaron’s. It is the LORD’s. The people are marked with his name, and the blessing is his gift to them.
connection: Samson, Samuel, and John the Baptist were set apart as Nazirites or in a similar way. Paul took a vow of this kind (Acts 18:18). Jesus is the greater one who was wholly consecrated to the Father. Paul prays a version of the blessing in his letters (2 Corinthians 13:14; Philippians 4:7). Hebrews 7:1 says that Melchizedek blessed Abraham, and Jesus lifted his hands and blessed his disciples as he ascended (Luke 24:50-51).
application:
Read the blessing aloud, and receive it as a word spoken over you personally. Then speak it over someone you love.

Think about whether there is something you need to confess and repay.

Consider what it would mean to set aside something for a season so that you could give more to God.
prayerPrompts: Pray the Aaronic blessing over yourself, slowly, in your own words.
Ask him to put his name on you and make you a blessing.
Pray the same blessing over someone you love.
